title: fix: distinguish invalid api keys from missing credentials in 401s
author: ElliotEtag
pr_body_excerpt:
- A request with an expired, revoked, or deleted API key returned the same 401 message as a request with no credentials at all ("Authentication required. Please provide an API key…"), which misreads as an auth-plumbing bug instead of a dead key.
- gen's auth middleware now notes when a key was extracted from the request but failed authentication, and `requireAuthorization`/`requireUser` return 401 "Invalid API key. The provided key was not recognized; it may be expired, revoked, or mistyped." with a pointer to https://enter.pollinations.ai/keys.
- The invalid-key message also takes precedence over route-specific "please provide a key" messages (realtime), since those are written for the no-credentials case.
- Adds a worker test asserting the invalid-key 401 body; existing 401 (no credentials), 402 (paidOnly balance), and 403 (permissions/banned) behavior is unchanged.

Context: a deleted testing key surfaced as "paidOnly models return 401 while openai works" — the non-paid models were only succeeding via pre-auth text-cache hits, and the generic 401 message hid that the key itself no longer existed.

gist.headline: The key knows it is dead
gist.blurb: Dead keys now say so. The hive stopped sending developers on a scenic tour of their authentication plumbing when the real problem was a revoked, expired, deleted, or mistyped key.
gist.summary: Gen authentication now distinguishes an invalid extracted API key from missing credentials, returning a 401 that says the key was not recognized and links to https://enter.pollinations.ai/keys while preserving existing no-credential 401, paid-only 402, and permission 403 behavior.
gist.impact: Developers with expired, revoked, deleted, or mistyped keys will get an actionable invalid-key 401 instead of a generic request-for-credentials message, including on realtime routes.
gist.visual_concept: Depict Polli as a careful little key gardener examining two keys at a cozy terminal: one healthy lime-green key accepted by a glowing lock, and one faded key clearly labeled invalid. A small CRT monitor robot can point helpfully toward a pixel sign reading “/keys,” while code-plants and flowers make the authentication diagnosis feel clear rather than alarming.
